title: Flu season arrives a month early as mutated H1N1 drives hospitalizations to a 16-year high
excerpt: The 2026-27 flu season has arrived about a month early in the United States, driven almost entirely by influenza A H1N1 — and federal surveillance shows hospitalizations at their highest level for this time of year since the 2010-11 season.
content:
The 2026-27 flu season has arrived about a month early in the United States, driven almost entirely by influenza A H1N1 — and federal surveillance shows hospitalizations running at their highest level for this time of year since the 2010-11 season.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's FluView report for the week ending Oct. 24 recorded about 6,100 lab-confirmed flu hospital admissions nationwide, up 27 percent from the week before. The hospitalization rate that week was the highest for that calendar week since the 2010-11 season. Of the influenza A viruses that public health labs subtyped that week, 98.9 percent were H1N1. The CDC estimated at least 1 million illnesses, 16,000 hospitalizations and 900 deaths so far this season, including the season's first pediatric death, linked to H1N1. More recent CDC estimates reported Nov. 5 put the season's toll at at least 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths.

Flu activity is growing or likely growing in 44 states, according to the CDC, and infections have been climbing since August — roughly two and a half months earlier than a typical season. Outpatient visits for flu-like illness reached 2.2 percent of visits during the week ending Oct. 17.

Researchers are watching a new mutation, called G155E, in the circulating H1N1 virus. It appeared in a subclade known as D.3.1.1, which researchers traced to Japan around May 2026 and first identified in U.S. samples in Seattle in September. The mutation sits at a position scientists know is important for generating protective antibody responses, and early laboratory findings suggest it may help the virus partly evade immunity from previous infections or vaccination. Andrew Pekosz, a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told TODAY.com it is not yet clear whether the mutation is contributing to the early surge or making infections more severe.

The CDC says it is too early to determine whether the mutation will affect how well this season's vaccine protects people, and current-season effectiveness numbers have not yet been published. Because this season's shot was formulated before G155E spread widely, it is being described as a partial rather than full match to the circulating strain.

The CDC also cautions that an early start does not necessarily mean a worse season overall: “an earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity.” Even so, CDC forecasters expect admissions to keep rising into mid-November, projecting 4,800 to 23,200 lab-confirmed flu admissions for the week ending Nov. 14.

The CDC recommends the flu vaccine for nearly everyone 6 months and older, and says October and November are the best months to get vaccinated — though vaccination in December or later still provides considerable protection. Flu shots are available at local clinics and pharmacies across Webb County. Webb Watch covered the early flu season on Oct. 21 and Oct. 25 and the season's first pediatric death on Nov. 1; this story updates those reports with the latest CDC numbers and the mutation findings.

Sources: CDC FluView, week 42 ending Oct. 24, 2026; CDC FluSight forecasts; TODAY.com / Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health; Nature World News; Health and Me, Nov. 10, 2026.

Update — November 14, 2026

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's FluView report for the week ending Nov. 7, published Friday, Nov. 13, shows the early flu season still climbing. Outpatient visits for flu-like illness reached 3.2 percent nationwide, above the 2.9 percent national baseline, and the share of flu tests coming back positive rose to 11.3 percent from 9.1 percent the week before, according to the CDC's weekly update summarized by CIDRAP. The CDC now estimates at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths so far this season. Two more children died of flu this week, bringing the season's pediatric death total to five. Seven states now show high or very high flu activity, up from two at the high level the week before, the Associated Press reported — and Texas is among them, with 4.8 percent of outpatient visits for flu-like illness in the week ending Nov. 7, the highest share in the state so far this season, according to CDC ILINet data. Dallas County reported a child's death from flu on Nov. 11, its first pediatric flu death since 2022, county health officials said. The CDC cautions that an early rise does not necessarily mean a higher seasonal peak, but activity remains higher than usual for this time of year.

Sources: CDC FluView, week 44 ending Nov. 7, 2026; CIDRAP, Nov. 13, 2026; Associated Press, Nov. 13, 2026; Texas Department of State Health Services, Texas Respiratory Virus Surveillance Report, Nov. 1–7, 2026; Dallas County Health and Human Services, Nov. 11, 2026.
